title: Self-Employment Taxes
subtitle: Turn irregular income into a tax system you can explain

blocks.text: Self-employment can mean freedom, extra income, or a side business that slowly grows into a full-time job. It also changes how tax reaches the government. No employer handles deductions in the background anymore. You report the income, back up the expenses, plan for tax and CPP or QPP, and keep records that still make sense months later.

That sounds heavier than it needs to be. This lesson isn’t trying to turn you into an accountant. It’s a simple system for capturing the right information, setting money aside and knowing when to pay a professional.

This is general Canadian education for people who work for themselves. It isn’t personal tax, legal or business advice. Rules, deadlines and provincial requirements change, so confirm anything time-sensitive with the CRA, Revenu Québec where it applies, or a qualified professional. You’ll build one clean business tax file as you go, to replace the yearly shoebox ritual with a routine that takes minutes, not a weekend and three increasingly worried coffees.

items.title: “A side hustle is too small to report.”
items.text: Business income doesn’t get a costume labelled “hobby money” just because it arrived after regular work hours. Report it, then work out which supported expenses you can deduct.

blocks.text: Keep more of what your business earns, and never dread April again.
blocks.detail: A simple monthly routine turns tax season from a scramble into a short meeting with your numbers.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows the four places every payment should go.

blocks.text: Self-employment income can come from almost any work you do for yourself to make a profit: contract jobs, freelance work, online sales, repairs, care work, art, delivery or sales commissions. A business doesn’t become invisible because it’s part-time, paid through an app or run from a kitchen table.

Start with two different numbers. Gross income is everything the business brought in before expenses. Net income is what’s left after eligible business expenses come off. Gross shows the size of the activity. Net is what’s generally used for taxable income and for self-employed CPP.

Record every sale or fee: invoices, platform statements, payment reports, bank deposits and cash sales. If a client pays in another currency, keep the original invoice, the Canadian-dollar amount you reported and where you got the exchange rate.

Don’t report only what landed in the bank after a platform took its cut. Record the full customer payment as income, and the platform’s fee as its own expense. Netting the two together hides the real sale. Since 2024, many online platforms also report their sellers’ income straight to the CRA.

The law doesn’t always require a separate bank account for your business, but one makes your records much clearer. It’s one less argument with yourself about whether a hardware-store charge was for shelving or a suspiciously ambitious barbecue.
Employee or self-employed?

The label in a contract isn’t the whole answer. What matters is the working relationship: who controls the work, who owns the tools, whether you can make a profit or take a loss, how much you’re part of their business, and whether you can hire help. Quebec has its own related rules for provincial purposes.

Getting this wrong can affect income tax, CPP or QPP, Employment Insurance, payroll and your rights as a worker. If it’s unclear, get professional advice or ask the CRA for an official ruling. A confident title on an invoice doesn’t settle the law.

A sole proprietor and the business are generally the same taxpayer. Moving money from the business account to your personal account is an owner’s withdrawal, not a deductible salary. Your business result comes from income and eligible expenses, not from how much you moved home.

items.title: OPERATING MONEY
items.text: Pays the everyday costs of running the business: supplies, tools, ads and regular bills.

items.title: TAX RESERVE MONEY
items.text: Sets aside what income tax and CPP or QPP will need later. This is the lane that stops a good year from turning into a rough April.

items.title: GST/HST MONEY
items.text: Once you’re registered, this holds the tax you collected from customers. It was never yours to spend. You’re just holding it.

items.title: OWNER MONEY
items.text: What’s left for personal use, after the first three lanes are covered.

blocks.text: These don’t need to be four bank accounts. They do need to be four separate amounts in your records. GST/HST you collect is never profit. And tax reserve money shouldn’t become emergency ad money because an ad promised to “change everything by Tuesday.”

Move money to the tax reserve every time a customer pays you. The right share depends on your total income, province or territory, deductions, credits and whether a job already takes tax off your pay. A tax professional can help you estimate it. Many people start with 25% to 30% of each payment and adjust after their first return. The habit that matters is setting the money aside before you decide what to spend.

sections.title: Claim the Business Part, Not the Hopeful Part

blocks.text: Form T2125, Statement of Business or Professional Activities, is what sole proprietors commonly use to report business income and expenses with their personal return. It lays out gross income, types of expenses and net income.

The general idea is simple: a reasonable expense you pay to earn business income may be deductible, subject to specific limits. Personal expenses aren’t. Equipment that lasts, called capital property, is usually deducted a piece at a time through capital cost allowance, not all at once.

Common costs include ads, business insurance, office costs, fees for an accountant or lawyer, supplies, work travel, bank fees, interest, rent, wages, delivery and the work share of your phone and internet. The category name doesn’t make a claim valid. The business purpose and the record behind it do.

items.title: MIXED PERSONAL AND BUSINESS USE
items.text: When a cost serves both purposes, claim only the business share you can support. For a phone or internet plan, use a reasonable method based on real business use, and write the method down, so next year’s math doesn’t depend on memory and optimism.

items.title: CURRENT EXPENSES VS. CAPITAL PROPERTY
items.text: An ordinary supply is usually used up within the year. Capital property lasts longer and supports the business over time, so a printer cartridge and the printer itself can be treated differently for tax. Record the date, description, seller, cost, tax paid and business use, and let the facts decide.

items.title: “If I have a receipt, the expense is deductible.”
items.text: A receipt proves money changed hands. It doesn’t prove the purchase had a business purpose. A crisp receipt for a personal television is still a personal television.

blocks.text: Home office expenses have their own rules. The space must be your main place of business, or used only to earn business income and to meet clients on a regular basis. Use the T2125 calculation, and get advice before you claim a room just because a laptop once visited it.

Vehicle claims need proof too: total kilometres, business kilometres, trip dates, destinations, the business reason and receipts for running costs. Driving from home to your regular place of business may count as personal commuting, while travel between business locations can be treated differently. The facts matter.

The CRA allows a shorter logbook in some cases, but only after you keep a full logbook for one whole year first. After that base year, you can keep a log for a sample three months each year, as long as your driving pattern stays similar. Keep the base-year log as proof.
Malik creates Tax Friday
paragraphs: Malik lived in Winnipeg. He repaired bikes on weekends and did graphic design during the week. Customers paid him by e-transfer, cash and an online platform. In his first year, he watched his bank balance and assumed it was profit.

By April, reality arrived. His income showed up in three places, his receipts were scattered across five and he had set nothing aside for tax. His first tax bill came to $6,200, plus CPP he hadn’t known he owed. He paid it with a credit card and a knot in his stomach.

A friend suggested costly accounting software that promised to “do it all.” Malik was tempted. Instead, he chose something smaller he knew he would stick with. He opened a separate chequing account, made folders for sales and expenses and named the first Friday of every month Tax Friday.

On Tax Friday, he downloaded platform statements, matched deposits to invoices, photographed receipts, logged his kilometres and moved 25% of the month’s income into a tax reserve. He also cleaned up his claims. Personal meals came out. His phone and van costs were split into business and personal shares. When he bought a professional truing stand, he flagged it as equipment instead of deducting it all at once.

The twist came the next spring. The CRA sent him a reminder to pay tax in instalments, since his tax owing was now over $3,000. A year earlier it would have panicked him. Now his tax reserve already held the money, and he set up the four quarterly payments in ten minutes.

At year-end, Malik still met with a tax professional, but he showed up with organized records and clear questions instead of a shoebox. The meeting was about decisions, not archaeology. His bank balance had stopped pretending to be four different numbers at once.

blocks.text: An hour a month buys you a calm tax season and a clearer view of your real profit.
blocks.detail: Setting money aside as it arrives means every tax bill is already paid before it shows up.
blocks.extra: Section 06 lays out the dates and amounts to plan for.

sections.title: Plan for Tax Before the Deadlines Arrive

blocks.text: Self-employed people get a later filing deadline than most taxpayers, but any balance owing is due earlier. For the 2025 return, the self-employed filing deadline was June 15, 2026, while any tax owing was due April 30, 2026. Check the current year’s dates before you act.

items.title: “Self-employed people can wait until the June filing deadline to pay.”
items.text: Filing and paying run on different clocks. A later filing deadline doesn’t move the date your balance is due.

blocks.text: File on time even if you can’t pay in full. Interest and late-filing penalties are separate problems, and the CRA may offer a payment arrangement. Silence is not a payment plan.
CPP or QPP contributions

An employee and their employer normally split CPP contributions. A self-employed person pays both shares through their personal tax return, based on net business income within the yearly limits. Quebec residents use QPP rules instead. That’s one reason a tax reserve needs more room than a rough income-tax estimate suggests.
Self-employed CPP in 2026

items.title: First layer
items.text: 11.9% — of net business income between $3,500 and $74,600. The most you pay is $8,460.90.

items.title: Second layer (CPP2)
items.text: 8% — of net business income between $74,600 and $85,000. The most you pay is $832.

items.title: Tax relief
items.text: Part deducted, part credited — the employer half and the enhanced part reduce your taxable income.

blocks.text: Self-employed CPP is worked out on net business income, not on every dollar deposited. Expenses can lower net income, but they don’t turn a needless purchase into free money. Spending a dollar to save tax on part of that dollar is still spending.
Income tax instalments

You must pay tax in instalments if your net tax owing is more than $3,000 ($1,800 in Quebec) this year and was also over that in either of the two years before. Instalments are due March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15. They’re advance payments toward the year’s tax, not an extra tax. The CRA mails reminders in February and August with suggested amounts. If you pay those amounts on time, the CRA won’t charge instalment interest, even if your final tax turns out higher. Keep proof of every payment.
Put income-tax instalment dates in your calendar separately from GST/HST filing dates. Two government deadlines can share a month without being the same obligation.

Income tax and GST/HST registration are two separate questions. You can owe income tax without being registered for GST/HST. Registration depends on your sales, what you sell, where and some special rules. The next lesson covers it.

sections.title: Build Records That Answer Three Questions

blocks.text: A useful record system should answer three questions.

items.title: What income did the business earn?
What supported costs did it pay to earn that income?
Which tax payments, instalments or collected sales tax belong to this period?

blocks.text: Make a folder for each tax year. Inside, keep separate folders for sales, expenses, bank and payment statements, vehicle logs, home office math, equipment purchases, contracts, tax payments and filed returns. Use file names that include the date, the supplier or customer and the purpose.

Check your records against your business bank and platform statements every month. A missing receipt is easier to chase after thirty days than after eleven months. If a supplier never gave you a receipt, write down their name and address, the amount, the date and what you bought, and keep any other proof you have.

items.title: “Bookkeeping software makes the records correct.”
items.text: Software can add up what it’s given. It can’t know a deposit is missing, a personal purchase got the wrong label or the same receipt was uploaded twice. Checking against the bank is where a person makes sure the tidy screen matches real life.

blocks.text: The CRA generally wants business records kept for six years from the end of the last tax year they relate to, with special rules in some cases. Electronic records must stay readable and easy to reach. A faded receipt photographed today beats a blank strip of thermal paper next year.
Cloud storage is a backup location, not a filing system on its own. A folder called “Tax stuff FINAL final 2” may be emotionally honest, but it won’t explain which invoice belongs to which sale.

Protect the sensitive files with strong passwords, two-step login and limited access to account numbers, SINs, customer data and tax documents. A bookkeeper or software company can help keep records, but you’re still responsible for having them ready when the CRA asks.

sections.title: What Changes by Province or Territory

blocks.text: Federal tax and CPP work the same in most of Canada, but your province or territory adds its own tax, which changes the final number. Quebec residents generally deal with Revenu Québec for provincial income tax and QPP, often with separate forms and deadlines.

Business registration, licences, workers’ compensation, payroll and sales taxes can vary too. British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec run their own provincial sales taxes alongside GST. Ontario and the Atlantic provinces use HST, while Alberta and the territories have no provincial sales tax. What you sell, where your customer is and where your business operates can all change the answer.

Write down your main business location, every province or territory where you often work or sell, and whether you have staff, stock or property elsewhere. Take that list to a qualified adviser. A business can cross a tax border online without anyone packing a suitcase.
Key takeaway

Self-employment tax becomes manageable once your money and records each have a job. Record gross income, claim only the supported business share of expenses, set aside money for income tax and CPP or QPP, watch for instalments and GST/HST, and close your records every month. Good organization doesn’t remove tax. It removes the surprises you could have avoided.

Close each month before starting the next: confirm sales, sort expenses, review unpaid invoices, update mileage, move money to the tax reserve and note one question to follow up. A twelve-minute checklist used often beats a beautiful yearly one used never.

items.title: What’s the difference between gross and net business income?
items.detail: Gross is all business income before expenses. Net is what’s left after eligible business expenses come off.

items.title: Why isn't an owner's personal withdrawal a deductible salary expense for a sole proprietor?
items.detail: A sole proprietor and the business are generally the same taxpayer. The result comes from income and eligible expenses, not from how much the owner moved to a personal account.

items.title: What does a receipt prove, and what doesn’t it prove?
items.detail: It proves a purchase happened. On its own, it doesn’t prove a business purpose, or that the full amount is deductible.

items.title: Why can the filing deadline and the payment deadline cause confusion?
items.detail: Self-employed people can file their return later but still owe any balance by the normal payment date. The two clocks run separately.

items.title: Name three records that can support a business vehicle claim.
items.detail: For example: total kilometres, work kilometres, trip dates, where you went, why you went and receipts for gas and repairs.

sections.title: Your Action: Build Your Monthly Tax-File Routine

blocks.text: Answer these six questions using estimates where you need to. This is preparation, not a final tax calculation.
This exercise isn’t about landing on a final tax bill. It’s about building records the bill can be worked out from. Leave SINs, full account numbers and tax documents out of this form.

items.title: Capital cost allowance (CCA)
items.text: The tax system for deducting the cost of lasting equipment and property over several years.

items.title: Current expense
items.text: An everyday cost of earning income this year, subject to tax rules.

items.title: Gross business income
items.text: All business income before expenses come off.

items.title: Income tax instalment
items.text: A tax payment made during the year, required when not enough tax is taken off at source.

items.title: Mixed-use expense
items.text: A cost that serves both business and personal purposes.

items.title: Net business income
items.text: Business income left after eligible expenses. It’s used to work out taxable income and self-employed CPP.

items.title: Owner's withdrawal
items.text: Money an owner takes out of the business for personal use. It isn’t a business expense.

items.title: Self-employed person
items.text: Someone who runs a business on their own account, not as an employee.

items.title: Sole proprietor
items.text: One person who owns a business that isn’t incorporated and reports its results on their personal return.

items.title: T2125
items.text: The CRA form commonly used to report business or professional income and expenses.
